verses.t: Mencius said, "Favorable seasons from Heaven are not as good as advantages of terrain, and advantages of terrain are not as good as harmony among people. Suppose there is a town with an inner wall three li around and an outer wall seven li around. It is surrounded and attacked, but not taken. In surrounding and attacking it, the attackers must have had a favorable season at some point; that they still could not take it shows that favorable seasons are not as good as advantages of terrain. Suppose the walls are not lacking in height, the moats are not lacking in depth, the weapons and armor are not lacking in strength and sharpness, and the stores of grain are not lacking in quantity; yet the defenders abandon the place and flee. This shows that advantages of terrain are not as good as harmony among people. So it is said: people are not kept in by the boundaries of borders, a state is not made secure by the barriers of mountains and ravines, and the world is not overawed by the sharpness of weapons and armor. One who has found the Way has many to help him; one who has lost the Way has few to help him. When help is at its fewest, even his own kin turn against him; when help is at its most, the whole world follows him. With the whole world following him, he attacks one whom even his own kin have turned against. Therefore the gentleman may choose not to fight; but if he fights, he is sure to win."

Mencius was about to go to court to see the king, when the king sent a messenger to say, "I was intending to come and see you, but I have a chill and must not expose myself to the wind. Tomorrow morning I shall hold court; I wonder whether you will let me see you then?" Mencius replied, "Unfortunately I too am ill and cannot come to court." The next day he went out to pay a condolence call on the Dongguo family. Gongsun Chou said, "Yesterday you declined on the grounds of illness, and today you go to pay a condolence call. Is that perhaps not proper?" Mencius said, "Yesterday I was ill; today I am better. Why should I not pay a condolence call?" The king sent someone to ask about his illness, and a physician came. Meng Zhongzi replied to them, "Yesterday, when the king's summons came, he had a slight indisposition and could not go to court. Today he is a little better and has hurried off to court. I do not know whether he will have arrived yet." Then he sent several men to intercept Mencius on the road and tell him, "Please do not come home; go to court." Mencius had no choice but to go and spend the night at the house of Jing Chou. Jingzi said, "Within the home, there is the relation of father and son; outside it, the relation of ruler and minister. These are the great relationships of humankind. Between father and son kindness is the chief thing; between ruler and minister respect is the chief thing. I have seen the king show respect to you, but I have not seen how you show respect to the king." Mencius said, "Oh! What kind of thing is that to say! Among the people of Qi there is no one who speaks to the king about humaneness and righteousness. Is it because they think humaneness and righteousness are not fine things? It is because in their hearts they say, 'How is he worth speaking to about humaneness and righteousness?' There is no greater disrespect than that. I do not dare to set anything before the king except the Way of Yao and Shun. So no one in Qi shows the king as much respect as I do." Jingzi said, "No, that is not what I meant. The Rites say: 'When your father calls you, do not answer with a slow "yes"; when your ruler's command summons you, do not wait for the horses to be harnessed.' You were certainly going to court, but when you heard the king's command you did not go after all. That seems not to accord with the Rites." Mencius said, "Is that what you mean? Zengzi said, 'The wealth of Jin and Chu cannot be matched. But they have their wealth, and I have my humaneness; they have their rank, and I have my righteousness. In what am I lacking?' Would Zengzi have said that if it were not right? There is a way of looking at it. There are three things universally honored in the world: rank is one, age is one, and virtue is one. At court nothing equals rank; in the village nothing equals age; in helping the world and leading the people nothing equals virtue. How can someone who has only one of them treat with contempt a man who has the other two? Therefore a ruler who is going to accomplish great things must have ministers whom he does not summon. When he wishes to consult them, he goes to them. If he does not honor virtue and delight in the Way to this degree, he is not worth working with. So Tang first learned from Yi Yin and only then made him his minister, and so became a true king without great effort. Duke Huan first learned from Guan Zhong and only then made him his minister, and so became leader of the feudal lords without great effort. Now the states of the world are alike in territory and equal in virtue, and none can surpass the others. The reason is nothing else than that their rulers like to have as ministers men whom they can teach, and do not like to have as ministers men from whom they would receive teaching. Tang would not have dared to summon Yi Yin, nor Duke Huan Guan Zhong. If even Guan Zhong could not be summoned, how much less one who would not be a Guan Zhong?"

Chen Zhen asked, "Formerly, in Qi, the king offered you a hundred measures of fine gold and you would not accept it. In Song you were offered seventy yi and accepted it; in Xue you were offered fifty yi and accepted it. If your refusal before was right, then your acceptance afterward was wrong; if your acceptance afterward was right, then your refusal before was wrong. Master, you must accept one of these alternatives." Mencius said, "I was right in every case. In Song, I was about to set out on a long journey, and a traveler must be given a parting gift. The message said, 'A parting gift.' Why should I not have accepted it? In Xue, I had reason to be on my guard. The message said, 'We hear you need to be on your guard, so this is for weapons.' Why should I not have accepted it? But in Qi there was no occasion for it. To give a man a gift when there is no occasion is to bribe him. How can a gentleman be won with a bribe?"

Mencius went to Pinglu and said to its governor, "If one of your spearmen fell out of the ranks three times in a single day, would you get rid of him or not?" "I would not wait for three times." "Then you yourself have fallen out of the ranks many times. In years of calamity and famine, the old and feeble among your people were tossed into the ditches and gullies, and the able-bodied scattered to the four quarters, several thousands of them." The governor said, "That is not something I, Juxin, could have done anything about." Mencius said, "Suppose a man takes charge of another man's cattle and sheep to herd them for him. He must certainly look for pasture and fodder for them. If he looks for pasture and fodder and cannot find any, should he return them to the owner? Or should he stand by and watch them die?" "In that case the fault is mine, Juxin's." Another day Mencius had an audience with the king and said, "Of those who govern cities for Your Majesty I know five, and the only one who recognizes his own fault is Kong Juxin." And he told the king the conversation. The king said, "In that case the fault is mine."

Mencius said to Chi Wa, "You declined [the governorship of] Lingqiu and asked to be made chief criminal judge, and this seemed reasonable, since it would let you speak [to the king]. Now several months have passed. Have you not yet been able to speak?" Chi Wa remonstrated with the king, but his advice was not taken, so he resigned his office and left. The people of Qi said, "What he did for Chi Wa was good; what he does for himself, we do not know." Gongduzi told Mencius this. Mencius said, "I have heard that one who holds an office should leave if he cannot carry out its duties, and one whose responsibility is to give advice should leave if his advice is not heeded. I hold no office and have no responsibility to give advice. So in coming forward and withdrawing, have I not ample room to act as I please?"

Mencius was serving as a high minister in Qi and went to Teng on a mission of condolence. The king sent Wang Huan, the governor of Ge, as his assistant. Wang Huan saw Mencius morning and evening, but all along the road from Qi to Teng and back Mencius never once spoke with him about the business of the mission. Gongsun Chou said, "The position of a high minister of Qi is not a small one, and the road from Qi to Teng is not short. Why did you never once speak with him about the business, there and back?" Mencius said, "Someone had already taken charge of it. What was there for me to say?"

Mencius went from Qi to Lu for a burial [his mother's], and on his return to Qi he stopped at Ying. Chong Yu made a request: "The other day, not knowing how unworthy I was, you put me in charge of the carpenters' work. Since there was urgency, I did not dare to ask. Now I would like to ask: the wood seemed too fine." Mencius said, "In antiquity there were no fixed rules for the inner and outer coffins. In middle antiquity the inner coffin was made seven inches thick, and the outer coffin to match. This held from the Son of Heaven down to the common people. It was not merely for appearance's sake, but because only then could people fully satisfy their hearts. If one was not permitted [such coffins], one could not be satisfied; if one lacked the means, one could not be satisfied. When it was permitted and the means were there, the ancients all used them. Why should I alone not do so? Moreover, is there not some comfort to the heart in keeping earth from touching the body of the departed? I have heard that a gentleman will not stint on his parents for the sake of anything in the world."

Shen Tong, on his own account, asked, "May Yan be attacked?" Mencius said, "It may. Zikuai had no right to give Yan to another man, and Zizhi had no right to receive Yan from Zikuai. Suppose there were an officer here whom you liked, and without informing the king you privately gave him your own salary and rank, and he, without any command from the king, privately accepted them from you. Would that be acceptable? How is this different?" The people of Qi attacked Yan. Someone asked, "Is it true that you urged Qi to attack Yan?" Mencius said, "No. Shen Tong asked me, 'May Yan be attacked?' and I answered, 'It may.' He took this as approval and attacked it. If he had asked, 'Who may attack it?' I would have answered, 'One who is the agent of Heaven may attack it.' Suppose there is a murderer, and someone asks, 'May this man be put to death?' I would answer, 'He may.' If he asked, 'Who may put him to death?' I would answer, 'The chief criminal judge may put him to death.' Now this is one Yan attacking another Yan. Why should I have urged it?"

The people of Yan rebelled. The king said, "I feel very ashamed before Mencius." Chen Jia said, "Do not let it trouble Your Majesty. Who do you think was more humane and wise, yourself or the Duke of Zhou?" The king said, "Oh! What kind of thing is that to say?" Chen Jia said, "The Duke of Zhou appointed Guanshu to oversee [the people of] Yin, and Guanshu led Yin in rebellion. If he knew [this would happen] and appointed him anyway, he was not humane; if he did not know, he was not wise. Even the Duke of Zhou was not perfect in humaneness and wisdom; how much less Your Majesty! Let me go to see Mencius and explain it." He went to see Mencius and asked, "What kind of man was the Duke of Zhou?" "A sage of antiquity." "Is it true that he appointed Guanshu to oversee Yin, and Guanshu led Yin in rebellion?" "It is." "Did the Duke of Zhou know he would rebel when he appointed him?" "He did not know." "Then even sages make mistakes?" Mencius said, "The Duke of Zhou was the younger brother, and Guanshu was the elder brother. Was not the Duke of Zhou's mistake an understandable one? Moreover, when the gentlemen of antiquity made mistakes, they corrected them; when the gentlemen of today make mistakes, they persist in them. The mistakes of the gentlemen of antiquity were like eclipses of the sun and moon: all the people saw them, and when they corrected them, all the people looked up to them. The gentlemen of today not only persist in their mistakes, but go on to make excuses for them."

Mencius resigned his office and was about to return home. The king went to see him and said, "Formerly I wished to see you but could not. Then I had the chance to serve you, and the whole court was delighted. Now you are leaving me to go home. I wonder whether I may hope to see you again after this?" Mencius replied, "I did not dare to ask it, but it is certainly what I wish." Another day the king said to Shizi, "I wish to give Mencius a house in the middle of the capital and support his disciples with ten thousand zhong of grain, so that all the great officers and the people of the state may have a model to respect and follow. Why do you not speak to him for me?" Shizi asked Chenzi to pass this on to Mencius, and Chenzi told Mencius what Shizi had said. Mencius said, "Yes. But how should Shizi know that it cannot be done? If I wanted to be rich, would I decline a hundred thousand and accept ten thousand? Is that wanting to be rich? Ji Sun said, 'How strange Zishu Yi was! He sought office for himself, and when he was not employed he ought to have stopped there; but he had his sons and younger brothers made high ministers as well. Who does not want wealth and honor? But in the midst of wealth and honor he alone kept a private hilltop.' In antiquity, marketing was the exchange of what one had for what one lacked, and the officials merely supervised it. Then there was a base fellow who would always look for a tall hilltop and climb it, so as to look left and right and net all the profit of the market. Everyone thought him base, and so they began to tax him. The taxing of merchants began with this base fellow."

Mencius left Qi and spent the night at Zhou. A man who wished to detain him on the king's behalf came, sat down and spoke to him. Mencius did not answer, but leaned on his armrest and lay down. The visitor was displeased and said, "I purified myself overnight before I dared to speak to you, and you lie down and will not listen. I shall not presume to see you again." Mencius said, "Sit down, and I will explain it to you plainly. In former times, if Duke Mu of Lu had not kept someone at the side of Zisi [to convey his respect], he could not have made Zisi feel secure; and if Xie Liu and Shen Xiang had not had someone at the side of Duke Mu, they could not have felt secure themselves. You are concerned for an elder like me, yet you do not come up to the way Zisi was treated. Is it you who have broken with your elder, or your elder who has broken with you?"

When Mencius had left Qi, Yin Shi said to others, "If he did not know that the king could not become a Tang or a Wu, then he was not clear-sighted. If he knew he could not, and still came, then he was seeking favor. He came a thousand li to see the king, and because they did not agree he left; yet he stayed three nights before leaving Zhou. Why such dawdling? I am not pleased with this." Gaozi told Mencius. Mencius said, "How should Yin Shi understand me? Coming a thousand li to see the king was what I wished. Leaving because we did not agree, was that what I wished? I had no choice. When I stayed three nights before leaving Zhou, I still felt in my heart that it was too soon. I hoped the king might change. If the king changed, he would certainly call me back. When I had left Zhou and the king did not send after me, only then did my mind become wholly set on going home. But even so, how could I abandon the king? The king is still capable of doing good. If the king were to employ me, it would not be only the people of Qi who would have peace; all the people of the world would have peace. I hope the king will change; every day I look for it. Am I like those petty men who, when their advice to their ruler is rejected, become angry, show their resentment on their faces, and when they leave travel with all their strength for a whole day before they stop for the night?" When Yin Shi heard this he said, "I am truly a petty man."

When Mencius had left Qi, Chong Yu asked him on the road, "Master, you seem to look displeased. But the other day I heard you say, 'A gentleman does not complain against Heaven, nor blame other people.'" Mencius said, "That was one time; this is another. Every five hundred years a true king must arise, and in the interval there must be men who make their age renowned. From the beginning of the Zhou until now is more than seven hundred years. By the count, the time is past; judging by the circumstances, it is due. It is simply that Heaven does not yet wish to bring peace and order to the world. If it wished to bring peace and order to the world, in the present age who is there besides me? Why should I be displeased?"

Mencius left Qi and stayed at Xiu. Gongsun Chou asked, "Is holding office without accepting salary the way of antiquity?" Mencius said, "No. At Chong I was able to see the king. When I withdrew, I already intended to leave, and I did not wish to change that intention; so I did not accept salary. Then orders came for the army to be mobilized, and it was not a time when I could ask to leave. Staying long in Qi was never my intention."
